input: Draft a neighborhood noise complaint to the council

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The specific type of noise (construction, music, traffic, dogs, etc.) completely changes the content, the bylaws referenced, and the angle of the complaint.
Whether this is from a single resident or a group of neighbors affects the tone, authority, and opening of the letter — a collective complaint carries more weight and is worded differently.
How long the noise issue has been happening and how frequently determines whether the complaint reads as a first-time report or an escalation of an ongoing, documented problem.
Whether the user has already contacted the council or the noise source directly affects what steps have been exhausted and how urgent or escalatory the letter needs to be.
The required format — a formal letter, an online submission form, an email — shapes structure, length, and whether headers, addresses, and sign-offs need to be included.
The desired tone (firm and assertive vs. polite and collaborative) determines word choice and how strongly the user wants to demand action versus request it.
Knowing the specific outcome the user wants — a fine, an investigation, noise barriers, changed hours — lets the complaint close with a clear, concrete ask rather than a vague appeal.

gold.taskTitle: Draft a neighborhood noise complaint to the council
gold.taskDescription: Write a formal complaint letter or document directed at the local council about a noise issue in the user's neighborhood.

questions.title: What is the specific source or type of noise?
questions.description: Identify the exact noise cause — e.g., a construction site, a neighbor's music, barking dogs, a nearby venue — so the complaint targets the right issue and references relevant regulations.

questions.title: Is this complaint from you alone or multiple neighbors?
questions.description: Determine whether the letter is written on behalf of a single resident or a group, as collective complaints are structured and framed differently and carry more weight.

questions.title: How long has the noise been occurring and how often?
questions.description: Establish the duration and frequency of the problem so the complaint accurately conveys whether this is a new incident or a persistent, ongoing issue.

questions.title: Have you already reported this to the council or the noise source?
questions.description: Find out what prior steps have been taken, so the letter can reference failed attempts at resolution and position itself as an escalation if needed.

questions.title: Should this be a formal letter, email, or online form submission?
questions.description: Clarify the required format and delivery method so the document is structured correctly — with or without formal addresses, subject lines, or specific council form fields.

questions.title: Should the tone be firmly assertive or politely cooperative?
questions.description: Gauge whether the user wants to come across as demanding immediate action or as a reasonable resident seeking collaborative resolution, which shapes the entire voice of the letter.

questions.title: What specific action or outcome do you want the council to take?
questions.description: Pin down the concrete resolution being requested — such as an investigation, enforcement of noise limits, fines, or changed operating hours — so the complaint ends with a clear, actionable demand.
